argument_summary: Certification is not supportable as a clean controls-only exception. It is supportable on a caveated basis using the existing admissible record: aggregate readiness passed by 2.4 points, rehearsal showed no severity-one incidents, and deployment begins with staged monitoring and rollback; at the same time, the health-plan benefits support segment remains exposed and below target, so the packet should treat certification as defensible only if it is paired with contemporaneous model-card disclosure of that limitation. The unresolved point is not whether operational controls exist, but that the policy requires disclosure unless the exposed limitation is resolved or covered by approved risk acceptance.
claims_about_business_cost: Escalation is not necessary if the auditor is prepared to treat this as caveated rather than clean compliance, because the existing record already supports a bounded certification rationale tied to disclosure and monitoring. That preserves the release path without overstating what the controls prove.
claims_about_policy: The admissible policy record cuts against a pure rollout-controls rationale. The governing standard says rollout controls and post-launch monitoring mitigate a material model-card weakness only if the affected use case is excluded or reviewed risk acceptance exists; otherwise disclosure remains required when the affected segment stays exposed. On the current record, the strongest policy-consistent position is caveated compliance: certification anchored in aggregate readiness and deployment controls, with explicit launch-time model-card disclosure of the known limitation, and without relying on the unsigned risk-acceptance draft as satisfying the policy predicate.
concessions: The affected health-plan benefits support segment remains below target and is still included in the randomized initial cohort.
The current record does not support a clean claim that staged rollout, monitoring, and rollback alone satisfy policy.
The risk-acceptance draft is unsigned and incomplete, so it should not be treated as approved coverage for the exposed limitation.
The present defense depends on required launch-time model-card disclosure; absent that disclosure, the compliance case is materially weaker.
